• Sum-of-positions comparison is the fastest fallback for 'odd pair out' letter-cluster questions when a direct letter-shift pattern isn't obvious.

 

NOTE

 

• Recompute at least one 'alike' pair after finding the odd one out, to make sure your rule genuinely explains the other three.

question: P, Q, R, S, T and U are sitting around a circular table facing the centre. R sits on the immediate left of U. S sits second to the right of T. P sits second to the left of R. How many people sit between R and Q when counted from the right of R?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option C i.e. 1.

 

GIVEN

 

• 6 people P, Q, R, S, T, U around a circular table, facing the centre.

 

• R is immediate left of U; S is second to the right of T; P is second to the left of R.

 

SOLUTION

 

• Fix R at position 1 (clockwise numbering = to a person's right, since they face the centre).

 

• 'R is immediate left of U' ⇒ U is immediate right of R ⇒ U = position 2.

 

• 'P is second to the left of R' ⇒ P = R − 2 = position 5 (going 2 steps counter-clockwise from R).

 

• Remaining positions 3, 4, 6 are for Q, S, T. 'S is second to the right of T' ⇒ position(S) = position(T) + 2. Testing T = 4, S = 6 works (both free); then Q = 3.

 

• Final clockwise order: 1=R, 2=U, 3=Q, 4=T, 5=P, 6=S.

 

• 'Counted from the right of R' means moving clockwise from R: the next seat is U (position 2), then Q (position 3). So 1 person (U) sits between R and Q along this path.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option C.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• For 'facing the centre' circular puzzles, fix one person's position, treat clockwise = their right and counter-clockwise = their left, and place every other clue relative to that fixed point before answering the final question.

 

NOTE

 

• Always double check which direction ('from the right of R' vs 'from the left of R') the final question asks you to count in — the answer often differs between the two.

question:
In a certain code language,

A + B means 'A is the daughter of B',

A − B means 'A is the brother of B',

A x B means 'A is the wife of B' and

A ÷ B means 'A is the father of B'.

Based on the above, how is D related to J if 'D + F − G ÷ H x J'?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option C i.e. Wife's father's brother's daughter.

 

GIVEN

 

• Code: A+B = A is daughter of B; A−B = A is brother of B; A×B = A is wife of B; A÷B = A is father of B.

 

• Expression: D + F − G ÷ H × J

 

SOLUTION

 

• D + F: D is the daughter of F.

 

• F − G: F is the brother of G (so F and G are siblings; F is male).

 

• G ÷ H: G is the father of H (so G is male, and H is G's child).

 

• H × J: H is the wife of J.

 

• So: G (father) and F (his brother) are siblings; H is G's daughter (since H later becomes someone's wife); D is F's daughter, so D and H are first cousins.

 

• From J's point of view: J's wife is H; H's father is G; G's brother is F; F's daughter is D.

 

• So D = J's Wife's father's brother's daughter.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option C.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• Decode the expression strictly left to right, writing a small family tree (or a chain of relations) as you go — this avoids losing track of who is whose sibling/child/spouse.

 

NOTE

 

• Always re-express the final relation strictly from the perspective named in the question (here, 'D related to J', so build the chain starting from J's wife and work outward).

question: Each of the digits in the number 3728645 is arranged in ascending order from left to right. What will be the sum of the digits that are second from the left and second from the right in the new number thus formed?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option D i.e. 10.

 

GIVEN

 

• Number: 3728645.

 

SOLUTION

 

• Digits: 3, 7, 2, 8, 6, 4, 5. Arranged in ascending order: 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8.

 

• Second digit from the left = 3. Second digit from the right = 7.

 

• Sum = 3 + 7 = 10.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option D.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• After sorting, the 'second from left' and 'second from right' positions are simply the 2nd and (n−1)th terms of the sorted list — read them off directly instead of re-counting from scratch.

 

NOTE

 

• List out every digit of the original number carefully before sorting — a single missed or duplicated digit will shift every subsequent position.

question: A man starts from Point A and drives 9 km towards north. He then takes a right turn, drives 15 km, turns right and drives 18 km. He then takes a right turn and drives 23 km. He takes a final right turn, drives 9 km and stops at Point P. How far (shortest distance) and towards which direction should he drive in order to reach Point A again? (All turns are 90 degrees turns only unless specified)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option B i.e. 8 km to the east.

 

GIVEN

 

• From A: 9 km North → right turn, 15 km → right turn, 18 km → right turn, 23 km → right turn (final), 9 km → stop at P.

 

SOLUTION

 

• (Method: track coordinates, start A = (0,0), facing North) 9 km North: (0, 9). Right turn ⇒ now facing East; 15 km East: (15, 9).

 

• Right turn ⇒ now facing South; 18 km South: (15, 9−18) = (15, −9).

 

• Right turn ⇒ now facing West; 23 km West: (15−23, −9) = (−8, −9).

 

• Right turn ⇒ now facing North; 9 km North: (−8, −9+9) = (−8, 0) = Point P.

 

• Distance from P(−8,0) to A(0,0) = 8 km. Since A's x-coordinate (0) is greater than P's (−8), A lies to the east of P.

 

• So he must drive 8 km to the east to reach A again.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option B.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• Track only the net (x, y) displacement using +/− steps for each direction (N=+y, S=−y, E=+x, W=−x) instead of drawing the full path — much faster for multi-turn direction problems.

 

NOTE

 

• For 'right turn' from facing North the new facing is East, then South, then West, then back to North — this 90° clockwise rotation cycle is worth memorising cold.

question: A, B, C, E, F, P and Q are sitting around a circular table facing the centre. A sits fourth to the left of C. P sits fourth to the right of B. Only two people sit between C and B when counted from the left of C. E is not an immediate neighbour of P or B. F is not an immediate neighbour of P. Who sits third to the right of Q?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option A i.e. F.

 

GIVEN

 

• 7 people: A, B, C, E, F, P, Q around a circular table, facing the centre.

 

SOLUTION

 

• Fix C at position 1 (clockwise = right, counter-clockwise = left).

 

• 'Only two people between C and B, counted from the left of C' ⇒ B is 3 steps counter-clockwise from C ⇒ B = 1 − 3 = position 5 (mod 7).

 

• 'A is fourth to the left of C' ⇒ A = 1 − 4 = position 4 (mod 7).

 

• 'P is fourth to the right of B' ⇒ P = 5 + 4 = position 2 (mod 7, since 9 mod 7 = 2).

 

• Remaining positions {3, 6, 7} are for E, F, Q. Neighbours of P(2) are positions 1, 3; neighbours of B(5) are positions 4, 6.

 

• 'E is not a neighbour of P or B' ⇒ E cannot be at 1, 3, 4 or 6 ⇒ from {3,6,7}, E must be 7.

 

• 'F is not a neighbour of P' ⇒ F cannot be at 1 or 3 ⇒ from remaining {3, 6}, F must be 6, leaving Q = 3.

 

• Final arrangement (clockwise): 1=C, 2=P, 3=Q, 4=A, 5=B, 6=F, 7=E.

 

• 'Third to the right of Q(3)' = position 3+3 = 6 = F.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option A.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• Place the most restrictive numeric clues first (fixed distances from a reference point), and save the 'is not a neighbour of' clues for last — they're best used to eliminate options among the few leftover seats.

 

NOTE

 

• With 7 (odd) people, remember position arithmetic wraps mod 7 — e.g., position 1 − 4 becomes position 4 after adding 7, not a negative number.

question: A, B, C, D, W, X and Y are sitting around a circular table facing the centre of the table. A sits third to the left of X. Only one person sits between X and C when counted from the left of C. Only two people sit between B and W when counted from the right of W. D is an immediate neighbour of B. Who sits third to the right of Y?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option B i.e. A.

 

GIVEN

SOLUTION

 

• Fix C at position 1. 'Only one person between X and C, counted from the left of C' ⇒ X = 1 − 2 = position 6 (mod 7).

 

• 'A is third to the left of X' ⇒ A = 6 − 3 = position 3.

 

• 'Only two people between B and W, counted from the right of W' ⇒ B = position(W) + 3.

 

• Remaining positions {2, 4, 5, 7} are for B, D, W, Y. Testing W = 2 gives B = 5 (both free — valid); testing W = 4 gives B = 7 (also free, second candidate).

 

• 'D is an immediate neighbour of B': for W=2,B=5 — remaining {4,7} for D,Y; neighbours of B(5) are 4 and 6(=X, taken), so D = 4 (valid), Y = 7.

 

• For W=4,B=7 — remaining {2,5} for D,Y; neighbours of B(7) are 6(=X,taken) and 1(=C,taken), so no valid D — this case is rejected.

 

• Final arrangement (clockwise): 1=C, 2=W, 3=A, 4=D, 5=B, 6=X, 7=Y.

 

• 'Third to the right of Y(7)' = position 7+3 = 10 mod 7 = 3 = A.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option B.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• When a distance-based clue (like B = W+3) gives more than one possible seat pair, hold both as candidates and use the remaining clue (neighbour condition) to eliminate the invalid one — don't guess.

 

NOTE

 

• Note that option B's printed value is the person named 'A' — don't confuse the option letter (B) with the person's name (A).

question:
Read the given statements and conclusions carefully. Assuming that the information given in the statements is true, even if it appears to be at variance with commonly known facts, decide which of the given conclusions logically follow(s) from the statements.

 

Statements:

Some mangoes are bananas.

No banana is a kiwi.

 

Conclusions:

(I): All bananas are mangoes.

(II): No mango is a kiwi.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option B i.e. Neither follows.

 

GIVEN

 

• Statements: Some mangoes are bananas (I-type). No banana is a kiwi (E-type).

 

SOLUTION

 

• Conclusion I ('All bananas are mangoes') is an illegal conversion of 'Some mangoes are bananas' into a universal statement — 'some A are B' never guarantees 'all B are A'. So Conclusion I does not follow.

 

• Conclusion II ('No mango is a kiwi'): since only 'some' (not all) mangoes are bananas, the mango-banana overlap is only partial. The mangoes that are not bananas are unconstrained by the second statement and could still be kiwis in some valid Venn diagram. So Conclusion II does not follow either.

 

• Since neither conclusion is guaranteed true in every possible diagram consistent with the statements, the answer is Neither follows.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option B.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• 'Some A are B' + 'No B is C' never yields a definite A-C relation — only the overlapping (B) part of A is guaranteed free of C; the rest of A is undetermined. Memorise this as a standard 'no valid conclusion' combination.

 

NOTE

 

• Always test a conclusion by trying to draw at least one valid Venn diagram where the statements hold true but the conclusion is false — if you can, the conclusion does not follow.

question:
Read the given statements and conclusions carefully. Assuming that the information given in the statements is true, even if it appears to be at variance with commonly known facts, decide which of the given conclusions logically follow(s) from the statements.

 

Statements:

All Zucchinis are Leeks.

All Leeks are Radishes.

Some Radishes are Celeries.

 

Conclusions:

(I) All Leeks are Celeries.

(II) Some Radishes are Zucchinis.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option B i.e. Only conclusion (II) follows.

 

GIVEN

 

• Statements: All Zucchinis are Leeks. All Leeks are Radishes. Some Radishes are Celeries.

 

SOLUTION

 

• Chaining the first two universal statements: All Zucchinis are Leeks, and All Leeks are Radishes ⇒ All Zucchinis are Radishes.

 

• Conclusion I ('All Leeks are Celeries'): the third statement only says 'Some Radishes are Celeries' — since Leeks are only a part of Radishes, we cannot guarantee that the Celery-overlap portion of Radishes includes all (or even any) Leeks. So Conclusion I does not follow.

 

• Conclusion II ('Some Radishes are Zucchinis'): from 'All Zucchinis are Radishes' (a universal affirmative, A-type), by simple conversion we can validly derive 'Some Radishes are Zucchinis' (since the Zucchini class is non-empty). So Conclusion II follows.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option B.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• 'All A are B' always converts validly to 'Some B are A' (as long as A is a real, non-empty class) — apply this instantly whenever a universal statement is given and a 'some' conclusion in reverse order is offered.

 

NOTE

 

• Chain universal ('All X are Y') statements freely to build longer valid relations, but never assume a 'some' statement extends to cover a larger class than what it explicitly states.

question:

question:
Seven boxes, A, B, C, D, I, J and K, are kept one over the other, but not necessarily in the same order.

Only two boxes are kept between A and C. Only B is kept above K. No box is kept below C. J is kept at some place below D but at some place above I.

Which box is kept third above I?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option C i.e. D.

 

GIVEN

 

• 7 boxes A, B, C, D, I, J, K, stacked one over the other.

 

SOLUTION

 

• (Method: number positions 1 = bottom to 7 = top) 'No box is kept below C' ⇒ C is at the very bottom ⇒ C = 1.

 

• 'Only two boxes between A and C' ⇒ they are 3 positions apart ⇒ A = 4.

 

• 'Only B is kept above K' ⇒ exactly one box (B) is above K ⇒ K is second from top, B is at the top ⇒ K = 6, B = 7.

 

• Remaining positions {2, 3, 5} are for D, I, J. 'J is below D but above I' ⇒ order must be I < J < D. Assign the smallest to I, middle to J, largest to D ⇒ I = 2, J = 3, D = 5.

 

• Final stack (bottom to top): 1=C, 2=I, 3=J, 4=A, 5=D, 6=K, 7=B.

 

• 'Third above I(2)' = position 2 + 3 = 5 = D.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option C.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• Convert 'no box below X' and 'only Y above X' clues into fixed positions (bottom/near-top) immediately — they anchor the whole stack and make every other clue easy to place relative to them.

 

NOTE

 

• 'Third above I' means counting 3 positions upward from I's position, not 3 boxes physically between them — a subtle wording distinction worth double-checking.

question: If 1 is added to each odd digit and 2 is subtracted from each even digit in the number 51784563, then how many digits will appear more than once in the new number thus formed?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option D i.e. Three.

 

GIVEN

 

• Number: 51784563. Rule: odd digit → +1; even digit → −2.

 

SOLUTION

 

• Apply the rule digit by digit: 5(odd)+1=6; 1(odd)+1=2; 7(odd)+1=8; 8(even)−2=6; 4(even)−2=2; 5(odd)+1=6; 6(even)−2=4; 3(odd)+1=4.

 

• New number: 6 2 8 6 2 6 4 4.

 

• Count frequency of each digit: 6 → 3 times; 2 → 2 times; 8 → 1 time; 4 → 2 times.

 

• Digits appearing more than once: 6, 2 and 4 — that is three digits.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option D.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• Apply the transformation digit-by-digit in one pass and write the new number directly below the old one — this avoids mixing up which rule (add/subtract) applies to which digit.

 

NOTE

 

• The question asks for the count of distinct digits that repeat, not the count of repeated occurrences — don't confuse total repeats (3+2+2=7 occurrences) with distinct repeating digits (3).

question:
Select the set in which the numbers are related in the same way as are the numbers of the following sets.

(NOTE: Operations should be performed on the whole numbers, without breaking down the numbers into their constituent digits. E.g. 13 – Operations on 13 such as adding to/subtracting from/multiplying with 13 can be performed. Breaking down 13 into 1 and 3 and then performing mathematical operations on 1 and 3 is not allowed.)

 

(5, 22, 26)

(11, 40, 44)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option B i.e. (16, 55, 59).

 

GIVEN

 

• Sets: (5, 22, 26) and (11, 40, 44).

 

SOLUTION

 

• Test the relation: second number = 3 × (first number) + 7.

 

• Set 1: 3×5+7 = 15+7 = 22 ✓. Set 2: 3×11+7 = 33+7 = 40 ✓.

 

• Third number = second number + 4: Set 1: 22+4=26 ✓. Set 2: 40+4=44 ✓.

 

• So the rule is: (a, 3a+7, 3a+11). Check each option with this rule:

 

• Option A (13,32,36): 3×13+7 = 46 ≠ 32 — fails.

 

• Option B (16,55,59): 3×16+7 = 55 ✓; 55+4 = 59 ✓ — matches fully.

 

• Option C (17,58,54): 3×17+7 = 58 ✓ for the 2nd term, but 58+4 = 62 ≠ 54 — fails.

 

• Option D (16,66,70): 3×16+7 = 55 ≠ 66 — fails.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option B.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• With two given example sets, first nail the first-to-second number relation (try ×2,×3,+k combinations), then the second-to-third relation (often a small constant addition) — verify both against both given sets before testing the options.

 

NOTE

 

• Option C is a deliberate trap: it satisfies the first relation (3a+7) but fails the second (+4) — always verify every part of the pattern, not just the first one you find.

question:

Only A is kept above I. Only two boxes are kept between I and C. Only K is kept below J.

D is not kept immediately above C.

solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option C i.e. Two.

• 7 boxes A, B, C, D, I, J, K, stacked one over the other.

 

SOLUTION

• 'Only two boxes between I and C' ⇒ they are 3 apart ⇒ C = 6−3 = 3.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option C.

question:

solution_text:

• 223 × 4 − 164 ÷ 2 + 37 = ?

• 892 − 82 + 37 = 810 + 37 = 847.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option A.

question: YPMG is related to VKJB in a certain way based on the English alphabetical order. MVAM is related to JQXH. To which of the following options is DGRX related, following the same logic?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option C i.e. ABOS.

 

GIVEN

 

• YPMG : VKJB :: MVAM : JQXH :: DGRX : ?

 

SOLUTION

 

• Convert YPMG to numbers: Y=25,P=16,M=13,G=7. Convert VKJB: V=22,K=11,J=10,B=2.

 

• Differences: 22−25=−3; 11−16=−5; 10−13=−3; 2−7=−5. Pattern: −3, −5, −3, −5.

 

• Verify with MVAM→JQXH: M=13,V=22,A=1,M=13 → J=10,Q=17,X=24,H=8; differences: 10−13=−3; 17−22=−5; 24−1=+23≡−3(mod26); 8−13=−5. Pattern confirmed.

 

• Apply −3,−5,−3,−5 to DGRX: D=4,G=7,R=18,X=24 → 4−3=1=A; 7−5=2=B; 18−3=15=O; 24−5=19=S.

 

• Result = ABOS.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option C.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• With 4-letter coded words, always check for an alternating two-step pattern (like −3,−5 here) across positions before assuming a single constant shift.

 

NOTE

 

• When a shift goes below 'A' (position 1), wrap around using mod 26 (e.g. A(1)−3 → 24+1−3, i.e. treat as 1−3+26=24=X) — this situation didn't arise here but is a common trap in similar questions.

question: In a certain code language, 'OVAL' is coded as '9573' and 'LAVS' is coded as '3657'. What is the code for 'S' in the given code language?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option D i.e. 6.

 

GIVEN

 

• OVAL → 9573; LAVS → 3657.

 

SOLUTION

 

• Compare the letters used: OVAL has letters {O, V, A, L}; LAVS has letters {L, A, V, S}. The letters L, A, V are common to both words, while O appears only in OVAL and S appears only in LAVS.

 

• Correspondingly, the digit sets are {9,5,7,3} for OVAL and {3,6,5,7} for LAVS. The digits 3, 5, 7 are common to both codes, while 9 appears only in OVAL's code and 6 appears only in LAVS's code.

 

• Matching unique letter to unique digit: since O is the only letter unique to OVAL and 9 is the only digit unique to OVAL's code, O = 9.

 

• Similarly, since S is the only letter unique to LAVS and 6 is the only digit unique to LAVS's code, S = 6.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option D.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• When two coded words share several letters, first spot the letter that appears in only one word and the digit that appears in only one code — they must correspond to each other, giving you an instant answer without decoding the whole cipher.

 

NOTE

 

• This 'unique letter ↔ unique digit' elimination trick is especially useful when the exact substitution order isn't obvious from direct position-matching.

question: Aman starts from Point M and drives 8 km towards the north. He then takes a left turn, drives 5 km, turns left and drives 13 km. He then takes a right turn and drives 5 km. He then takes a right turn and drives 16 km. He takes a final right turn, drives 10 km and stops at Point P. How far (shortest distance) and in which direction is Point P with respect to Point M? (All turns are 90-degree turns only unless specified.)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option C i.e. 11 km towards the north.

 

GIVEN

 

• From M: 8 km North → left turn, 5 km → left turn, 13 km → right turn, 5 km → right turn, 16 km → final right turn, 10 km → stop at P.

 

SOLUTION

 

• (Method: track coordinates, start M = (0,0), facing North) 8 km North: (0, 8). Left turn ⇒ now facing West; 5 km West: (−5, 8).

 

• Left turn ⇒ now facing South; 13 km South: (−5, 8−13) = (−5, −5).

 

• Right turn ⇒ now facing West; 5 km West: (−5−5, −5) = (−10, −5).

 

• Right turn ⇒ now facing North; 16 km North: (−10, −5+16) = (−10, 11).

 

• Final right turn ⇒ now facing East; 10 km East: (−10+10, 11) = (0, 11) = Point P.

 

• Distance from M(0,0) to P(0,11) = 11 km, and since P's y-coordinate (11) is greater than M's (0) on the same vertical line, P lies north of M.

 

• So Point P is 11 km towards the north of Point M.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option C.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• Track only the net (x, y) displacement using +/− steps for each direction (N=+y, S=−y, E=+x, W=−x); the final answer is simply the straight-line distance from the origin to the last point, read off directly since it landed exactly on the y-axis here.

 

NOTE

 

• Recompute the facing direction at every single turn (left/right alternately) rather than assuming a repeating cycle — a mix of left and right turns (as in this question) changes the facing differently each time.
